content: Ulmus rubra, commonly known as the Slippery Elm, is a species of elm tree native to eastern North America. Its range extends from southeastern North Dakota eastward to southern Quebec and southward to northern Florida and eastern Texas. While it bears a general resemblance to the American Elm, it is more closely related to the European Wych Elm, as evidenced by their similar floral structures. The Slippery Elm is less vulnerable to Dutch elm disease compared to many other elm species and exhibits a distinct branching pattern. Its heartwood is reddish-brown, which has earned it the alternative name Red Elm. Other common names include Gray Elm, Soft Elm, Moose Elm, and Indian Elm. This deciduous tree typically grows to a height of 10–20 meters, with a trunk diameter of up to 50 centimeters. Its leaves are 10–18 centimeters long, rough in texture, with a coarsely double-serrated margin and an asymmetrical base. The flowers appear in early spring before the leaves emerge, forming clusters of 10–20. The fruit is an oval-shaped winged samara, approximately 2 centimeters long, containing a single seed at its center. The Slippery Elm can be distinguished from the American Elm by the hairiness of its buds and twigs (the American Elm has smooth buds and twigs) and by its very short-stalked flowers. The Slippery Elm thrives in moisture-rich uplands but can also grow well in dry, intermediate soils. It is rarely cultivated outside the United States. Uses The Slippery Elm is a highly valuable tree with numerous applications. Its inner bark can be ground into a nutrient-rich gruel, which can sustain an individual for a short period. The bark contains mucilage, a substance that is highly effective in treating sore throats. When dried and ground into a powder, it can be prepared as a tea. Both the tea and the gruel are known to soothe the digestive tract, making them useful for conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and gastritis. There are no known contraindications for the use of Slippery Elm, as it primarily consists of mucilage and various nutrients, and it is not classified as a drug. Historically, the bark has also been used as an abortifacient. It was moistened with water and inserted into the cervix. This practice led to the implementation of elm stick laws in several U.S. states, which prohibited the sale of Slippery Elm bark pieces longer than a certain length. Due to this historical use, the sale of whole Slippery Elm bark is banned in several countries, including the United Kingdom. The fibrous inner bark is strong and durable, making it suitable for spinning into thread, twine, or rope. It has been used for bowstrings, ropes, jewelry, clothing, snowshoe bindings, woven mats, and even some musical instruments. The wood of the Slippery Elm is highly shock-resistant due to its interlocking grain, making it ideal for wagon wheel hubs. It is also used for crafting bows, as it is both strong and flexible. Once cured, the wood is excellent for fire-making using the bow drill method, as it produces a fine, flammable powder under friction. Cultivars No specific cultivars of Slippery Elm are currently known. Hybrid Cultivars In the 1960s, Ulmus rubra was used as a hybrid parent, resulting in the release of cultivars such as Coolshade, Lincoln, Rosehill, and possibly Willis. In later years, it was also utilized in the Wisconsin breeding program to produce hybrids like Repura and Revera, although neither appears to have been commercially released as of 2007.
